source_text:
Εἰ οὖν οὐκ ἔχει οὕτως, δέσποτα, διὰ τί λέγεις Οὐ
δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν, ἐὰν μή τι βλέπῃ τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα; Ἵνα τὴν Ἰουδαίων ὑπεκλύσω μανίαν τῶν νομιζόντων με ἀντινομοθετεῖν τῷ πατρί· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐγκαλοῦσί μοι περὶ τῆς λύσεως τοῦ σαββάτου, εἶπον ὅτι Ὁ πατήρ μου ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται, κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι, ἑκατέρωθεν τὸ ὁμότιμον δεῖξαι θέλων. Ἀλλ' οἱ πάντα ἄφρονες νομίσαντές με ἔργα ἔργοις ἐπιτειχίζειν καὶ γνώμῃ γνώμην ἀντεισάγειν ἐκινοῦντο πρὸς φθόνον· ὅθεν διορθούμενος αὐτῶν τὴν γνώμην ἔλεγον Οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν, ἐὰν μή τι βλέπῃ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα ἀντὶ τοῦ Τί μοι οἱ ἄκαιροι τοῦ σαββάτου χολᾶτε ἐξετασταί, ὅτι λύω τὸ σάββατον; Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀντιπολιτεύομαι τῷ πατρί, οὐ γὰρ αὐτὸς στῆσαι τὸ σάββατον θέλει κἀγὼ λῦσαι· οὐκ ἀπομάχομαι πρὸς αὐτόν, οὐ στασιάζω πρὸς τὴν γνώμην, οὐκ αὐτὸς θέλει, ἐγὼ δὲ ἕτερα βούλομαι· ἃ θέλει θέλω, ἃ βούλεται βούλομαι, ἃ ποιεῖ ποιῶ. Οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐκτὸς αὐτοῦ οὐ ποιῶ, οὐ θέλω, ὅτι εἰς ἀδύνατον καθιστῶν τὸν λόγον λέγω· Ἀμὴν λέγω οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν· οὐ γὰρ ἔχω κεχωρισμένην καὶ ἀποτετμημένην τοῦ πατρὸς γνώμην. Μιᾶς γὰρ οὔσης τῆς φύσεως, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ θελήματος, ἀνάγκη τὸ ἀποτέλεσμα ἓν ὑπάρχειν. Οὐ δύναται οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν, οὐ γὰρ δύναται ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς ποιῆσαί τι ὅλον αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔχων· ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί. Εἰ γὰρ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος ἀδιάκριτα ἔργα διὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν, καίτοι διῃρημένης τῆς φύσεως, ἄλλο μὲν σῶμα θνητόν, ἄλλο δὲ ἀθάνατος ψυχή, πῶς δύναται ἐμοῦ τε καὶ τοῦ πατρὸς διακριθῆναι τὰ ἔργα; Ὅπου βουλὴ καὶ λόγος καὶ γνῶσις καὶ σοφία καὶ φύσις καὶ θεότης μία, οὐ δύναται οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδὲν διὰ τὸ μὴ κεχωρίσθαι τοῦ πατρός, ἐὰν μή τι βλέπῃ τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα, τουτέστιν ἐὰν μὴ τὸν πατέρα θέλοντα ἴδῃ. Ὡς μιᾶς γὰρ καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς φύσεως σύνδρομον ἔχων τὸ θέλημα ἀποτελῶ τὰ γινόμενα· εἰ μὲν γὰρ σωματικὴν ἐξεπλήρουν τὴν ἐργασίαν, ἀνάγκη διανέμεσθαι τοῦ γινομένου τὴν κατασκευήν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ θέλησις ἐστὶν ἀρκοῦσα πρὸς τὴν τῶν μὴ 2 ὄντων παραγωγήν, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργία τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὸν υἱὸν οἶδε δημιουργὸν οὐκ ἐξωθουμένου τοῦ πνεύματος.
thought_title: Why the Son says he can do nothing of himself
orientation: An interlocutor asks Jesus why he said the Son can do nothing of himself, and Jesus answers that the saying was meant to calm Jewish rage, not to subordinate him to the Father.
pass_a_gloss: If therefore it is not so, master, why do you say, The Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing something? In order that I might weaken the madness of the Jews who think that I legislate against the Father; for since they accuse me concerning the loosening of the Sabbath, I said, My Father works until now, and I work, wishing to show the equal honor from both sides. But the utterly foolish ones, thinking that I build works against works and introduce opinion against opinion, were stirred to envy; whence, correcting their opinion, I was saying, The Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing something, instead of, Why do you untimely examiners of the Sabbath rage against me, because I loosen the Sabbath? But I do not oppose the Father, for he does not wish to establish the Sabbath and I to loosen it; I do not fight against him, I do not rebel against his opinion, he does not wish one thing and I will other things; what he wishes I wish, what he wills I will, what he does I do. For thus I do nothing outside of him, I wish nothing, because making the statement impossible I say: Amen I say, the Son cannot do anything of himself; for I do not have an opinion separated and cut off from the Father. For since the nature is one, since the will is one, it is necessary that the result be one. The Son therefore cannot do anything of himself, for he cannot do anything without the Father, having him whole in himself; for I am in the Father and the Father is in me. For if the works of soul and body are indistinguishable because of the union, although the nature is divided, the body being one thing, mortal, and the immortal soul another, how can the works of me and of the Father be distinguished? Where counsel and word and knowledge and wisdom and nature and divinity are one, the Son therefore cannot do anything of himself because he is not separated from the Father, unless he sees the Father doing something, that is, unless he sees the Father willing. For as of one and the same nature, having the will running together, I accomplish the things that come to be; for if I were fulfilling a bodily work, it would be necessary that the construction of what comes to be be distributed; but since willing is sufficient for the production of things that are not, for this reason also the creation of all things knows the Father and the Son as creator, the Spirit not being excluded.

choices.why: The verb means to loosen or relax from under; rendering as weaken preserves the sense of calming or defusing the Jews' madness.
The compound means to make laws in opposition; the rendering keeps the legal force of νομοθετεῖν and the opposition of ἀντι-.
The verb means to build a wall against, used metaphorically of setting works in opposition; the rendering keeps the military image.
The compound means to bring in one thing in place of or against another; the rendering keeps the opposition and the sense of introducing an opinion.
The verb means to act as a political opponent; rendering as oppose keeps the sense of opposition without importing modern political language.
The adjective means running together or concurrent; the rendering keeps the image of the will moving together with the Father's.

pass_b_english: “If that is not how it is, master,” someone says, “why do you say, ‘The Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing it’?”

Jesus answers: “To weaken the madness of the Jews who think I am legislating against the Father. Since they accuse me about the breaking of the Sabbath, I said, ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working’ (John 5:17), wanting to show equal honor from both sides. But those utterly foolish people thought I was building works against works and introducing one opinion against another, and they were stirred to envy. So to correct their opinion I said, ‘The Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing it’ (John 5:19). What I meant was this: ‘Why are you so angry with me, you ill-timed examiners of the Sabbath, because I break the Sabbath? I am not opposing the Father. It is not that he wants to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it. I am not fighting against him; I am not rebelling against his will. He does not will one thing while I wish something different. What he wills, I will; what he wishes, I wish; what he does, I do.’ For in this way I do nothing and will nothing outside of him. I make the statement impossible when I say, ‘Amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself.’ I do not have an opinion separated and cut off from the Father. Since the nature is one and the will is one, the result must also be one. So the Son cannot do anything of himself, because he cannot do anything without the Father, having the Father whole within himself: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (John 14:10). If the works of soul and body are indistinguishable because of their union—even though their nature is divided, the body being one thing, mortal, and the soul another, immortal—how can my works and the Father’s be distinguished? Where counsel and word and knowledge and wisdom and nature and divinity are one, the Son cannot do anything of himself because he is not separated from the Father, unless he sees the Father doing it—that is, unless he sees the Father willing it. Since I have a will that runs together with the Father’s one and the same nature, I accomplish what comes to be. If I were carrying out a bodily labor, the construction of what comes to be would have to be divided up. But since willing is sufficient to bring things that do not exist into being, for this reason the creation of all things knows the Father and the Son as creator, with the Spirit not excluded.”

problems.quote: I make the statement point to an impossibility
problems.source_quote: ὅτι εἰς ἀδύνατον καθιστῶν τὸν λόγον λέγω
problems.why: Misreads syntax: 'because I make the word/logos point to an impossibility'—but this is about Jesus' own statement being framed as impossible, not him making 'the statement' point. More critically, 'ἀδύνατον' here means 'impossibility' but the construction 'εἰς ἀδύνατον καθιστῶν τὸν λόγον' means 'rendering the statement/logos impossible' i.e., showing it would be impossible. The English 'I make the statement point to an impossibility' is awkward and misleading—it's not about pointing to impossibility but about the statement itself being framed as impossible/self-contradictory if understood otherwise.
problems.fix: because I am showing that the statement would be impossible
problems.ruling: Greek says the word is rendered impossible; English says it merely points to an impossibility, changing the clause meaning.

edits.old: because I make the statement point to an impossibility when I say
edits.new: because I am showing that the statement would be impossible when I say

fixed: Changed 'I make the statement point to an impossibility' to 'I am showing that the statement would be impossible' to reflect the source's 'εἰς ἀδύνατον καθιστῶν τὸν λόγον' (rendering the statement impossible), not pointing to an impossibility.

problems.quote: having the whole Father in himself
problems.why: Wrong subject: the Son has the whole Father in himself, not 'he' ambiguous. Also 'himself' should be 'myself' since Jesus speaks in first person throughout.
problems.fix: having the whole Father in myself
problems.ruling: Greek ἑαυτῷ is first‑person; English 'himself' misidentifies speaker, altering reference.

edits.old: having the whole Father in himself
edits.new: having the whole Father in myself

fixed: Changed 'having the whole Father in himself' to 'having the whole Father in myself' because Jesus speaks in the first person throughout this passage, and the source has 'ὅλον αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔχων' with the first-person subject implied by the surrounding speech.

problems.quote: having the whole Father in myself
problems.why: Misreads case/grammar: αὐτὸν refers to the Son, not the Father. 'Having himself whole in himself' or 'having the whole of himself in himself'—the Son has the whole of himself in himself, not the Father in himself.
problems.fix: having his whole self in himself
problems.ruling: Greek αὐτὸν = the Son, not the Father; misidentifies referent

problems.quote: I am not opposing the Father. He does not want to establish the Sabbath while I want to dissolve it.
problems.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ αὐτὸς στῆσαι τὸ σάββατον θέλει κἀγὼ λῦσαι
problems.why: The Greek says 'for he does not want to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it'—this is part of what Jesus denies, not what he affirms. The English makes it sound like a statement of fact ('He does not want...while I want') rather than a denial of a supposed opposition. The structure is 'I am not opposing the Father; for [it is not the case that] he wants to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it'.
problems.fix: It is not that he wants to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it
problems.ruling: Greek denies both actions; English asserts opposite contrast

edits.old: having the whole Father in myself
edits.new: having his whole self in himself

edits.old: He does not want to establish the Sabbath while I want to dissolve it.
edits.new: It is not that he wants to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it.

fixed: Changed 'having the whole Father in myself' to 'having his whole self in himself' because the Greek 'ὅλον αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔχων' has αὐτὸν referring to the Son, not the Father.

Changed 'He does not want to establish the Sabbath while I want to dissolve it.' to 'It is not that he wants to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it.' because the Greek 'οὐ γὰρ αὐτὸς στῆσαι τὸ σάββατον θέλει κἀγὼ λῦσαι' is a denial of a supposed opposition, not a statement of fact.

fixed.quote: having his whole self in himself
fixed.fix: having the Father whole within himself
fixed.note: αὐτὸν refers to the Father, as the John 14:10 quote that follows confirms; the English wrongly says the Son has his own whole self.

dismissed.why: The interlocutor addresses Jesus as 'master' (δέσποτα), but English 'someone says' obscures this vocative and the direct address to Jesus.
dismissed.note: The English keeps the address 'master' inside the question, so nothing is lost.

dismissed.quote: I am not rebelling against his will
dismissed.why: γνώμην here is 'opinion/judgment' not 'will'; earlier γνώμην was 'opinion'. Inconsistent within same passage.
dismissed.note: γνώμη can mean will or purpose, and 'will' fits the following 'He does not will one thing'.

polish.changed: Clarified that Jesus resumes speaking after the objector's question, fixed the garbled logic about the impossible statement, clarified that the will runs together with the Father's nature, changed 'untimely' to 'ill-timed', and kept all claims and Scripture references intact.

variants.text: the same things, not things of such a kind
the very things the Father works

notes.why: Greek hosautos is rendered 'in the same way' but later unpacked as 'same things not similar'; reader may not connect these.
notes.fix: Gloss first occurrence: 'in the same way (the same things, not merely similar ones)'.

notes.quote: To weaken the madness of the Jews
notes.why: Christ's voice resumes without clear marker after objector's question; reader loses track.
notes.fix: Add 'Christ replies:' or format as direct speech.

notes.quote: I do not have an opinion separated and cut off from the Father
notes.why: Pronoun shifts from third-person exposition to first-person as Christ without warning.

notes.quote: For in this way I do nothing and will nothing outside of him, because I am showing that the statement would be impossible when I say
notes.why: Contradictory: 'I do nothing outside of him, because I am showing that the statement would be impossible'—logic garbled.
notes.fix: Revise to: 'because I am showing that the opposite statement would be impossible'.

notes.quote: Since I have a will running together with one and the same nature, I accomplish what comes to be
notes.why: Ambiguous: 'one and the same nature' with whom? Grammar suggests the will has a nature.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'Since my will runs together with the Father's, one and the same nature producing...'

notes.quote: you untimely examiners of the Sabbath
notes.why: 'Untimely' is odd for Greek akairos; means 'ill-timed' or 'inappropriate', but 'untimely' suggests premature death.

notes.quote: "If that is not how it is, master," someone says
notes.why: Reader cannot tell if 'someone' is an objector or Amphilochius himself adopting a persona.
notes.fix: Clarify this is an imagined interlocutor speaking to Christ through Amphilochius.

notes.quote: "To weaken the madness of the Jews who think I am legislating against the Father.
notes.why: Sudden shift to first-person Christ voice without explicit marker; reader may think Amphilochius is speaking.
notes.fix: Add a marker like 'Christ answers: 'To weaken...'

notes.quote: I am showing that the statement would be impossible when I say
notes.why: Does not make sense as English; unclear what 'impossible' modifies.
notes.fix: Rephrase: 'I am showing that the statement is about impossibility when I say...'

notes.quote: 'I am in the Father and the Father is in me' (John 14:10)
notes.why: John 14:10 reads 'I am in the Father and the Father is in me' but the full quote 'the Father who remains in me does the works' is 14:10b.
notes.fix: Cite as John 14:10 or split the two clauses.
